items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

items.title: [thehackernews.com] Grok Build exposes 35,578 apps, leaking sensitive company data
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Security researchers found that 35,578 of 37,571 web apps built with SpaceXSI’s Grok Build, a chat-based app builder, were accessible without signing in, exposing business and personal information at SpaceXSI and 30 other organizations. Claroc, the security firm that found the apps, estimated that about one in 10 accessible apps contained internal or personal data and roughly 2% held material it rated high or critical in severity. Exposed material included a SpaceXSI sales map covering 594 strategic accounts, a hospital directory listing more than 3,500 employees, an intensive-care briefing about a patient and a timesheet with 18 users’ passwords in its code. The apps’ addresses were discoverable through searchable passive DNS records, and Grok Build preselected “Anyone with the link” as the sharing option in the researchers’ test. SpaceXSI removed 24 apps made by its own staff and X employees; Claroc said other users’ apps remained available and that it had begun contacting affected organizations.

Google said its Project Suncatcher prototype satellite has returned its first AI-generated response from orbit. The satellite ran the Gemma 4 model on a data center-class Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) and transmitted a haiku during a ground-station pass over Svalbard, Norway. The satellite launched on Oct. 1, and Google described the response as an early milestone in research into operating AI computing hardware in space. The experiment tests whether the hardware can function in orbit; it is not a deployed computing service. Google’s next tests will examine performance under thermal stress and radiation exposure. The company says a successful trial could lead to two interconnected satellites in 2027.

Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency (CSA) urged organizations on Nov. 6 to restrict internet access to operational technology controls, including refrigeration systems, after cyberattacks on supermarket cooling systems and French blood-storage equipment. CSA said it had received no reports of comparable incidents in Singapore. The Singapore Food Agency said the attacks had not disrupted the country’s food supply and it was checking with retailers and cold-chain warehouses. The advisory follows a Nov. 5 warning from five U.S. agencies that attackers are targeting industrial refrigeration controllers worldwide. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 said it found more than 5,000 internet-exposed devices from manufacturers named in a French cybersecurity advisory on Nov. 5-6; the firm cautioned that exposure alone does not show a device was vulnerable. Censys separately counted 6,695 exposed controllers on Oct. 9 and 3,124 still accessible on Nov. 5. European Union agencies said affected member states were investigating and sharing information after another wave of attacks on Nov. 1-2. The perpetrators remain unidentified. Pro-Russian groups have claimed responsibility, but those claims are unverified, and the Kremlin denied Russian involvement.

Reports on that incident did not establish a link to Crafty Falcon.

items.title: [thestar.com] McGill report finds deepfake network spreading false Canada-U.S. trade claims
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

A McGill University research centre says a network of nearly 300 TikTok and Instagram accounts has circulated more than 3,201 deepfake videos that drew 22.1 million views over three months. Many focused on Canada’s trade dispute with the United States. One widely viewed false story described a nonexistent 48-hour ultimatum from President Donald Trump and claimed Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by cancelling $8 billion in U.S. defence contracts. It appeared in 161 videos on 129 accounts and drew 5.1 million views. The report says the accounts promote misleading claims from both sides of the trade debate, while the network’s operators and purpose remain unknown. Researchers said posting patterns and some accounts’ Chinese-language settings or registrations in China point to activity outside North America, but they could not firmly attribute the network to anyone. The report says the accounts have not been monetized and could be building an audience for later use, testing a tool or operating on behalf of someone seeking to influence Canadians.

items.title: [sciencefeatured.com] Higher BMI over time linked to faster cognitive decline in older adults
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

A 24-year study of several thousand middle-aged and older Americans found that higher average body mass index (BMI) over time was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking. A team led by University of Georgia researcher Suhang Song reported the findings in the Journal of Neurology. The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began. The observational study cannot establish that higher weight causes cognitive decline or that weight loss would prevent it. The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity. The team called for further research into possible biological mechanisms and future interventions.

items.title: [biz.heraldcorp.com] U.S. banking regulators probe cyber risks after $6.3 billion theft from Binance
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

U.S. banking regulators asked banks about unusual activity and service disruptions after attackers stole more than $6.3 billion in assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance on Oct. 29. Federal Reserve and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency supervisors began their inquiries on Nov. 2, while banks examined whether the attack exposed weaknesses in their own systems. Attackers used a fraudulent job interview and malicious software to compromise Binance employees’ computers, then exploited an internal artificial-intelligence tool, Binance said. The FBI and Binance have attributed the theft to North Korea; Pyongyang denies responsibility, while blockchain investigators have linked it to the North Korean group TraderTraitor. South Korean authorities also began checks of financial firms, including a planned inspection of about 580 companies.

items.title: [doctorsonly.co.il] Three cardiac teams report aortic repair, heart pump and nerve block
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Doctors at Beilinson Hospital repaired a woman’s enlarged aortic arch without opening her chest, using an endovascular device tailored to her. The technique has been used in about 70 cases worldwide. In Warsaw, a hospital implanted its first left ventricular assist device, an artificial pump that supports the heart, and activated a heart-transplant waiting list. Separately, Chinese doctors reported treating a 53-year-old woman who had repeated dangerous arrhythmias after going into cardiac arrest during surgery for a leg fracture. After medication failed to stop the episodes, a left-sided nerve block was followed by a marked reduction in abnormal heart rhythms within about five minutes.
